title: Design and Analysis of Quantum Designated Verifier Signature Scheme
abstract: Designated Verifier Signatures (DVS) are an important variant of digital signatures that ensure only a specified verifier can validate a signature, while preserving non-transferability. With the advent of quantum computing, several quantum DVS schemes have been proposed to achieve quantum security. In this paper, we revisit the quantum DVS protocol of Xin et al. [Quantum Information Processing, 2022] and provide a structural cryptanalysis of its design. We show that the scheme admits an existential forgery under a chosen-message attack: given a valid quantum signature on one message, an adversary can efficiently transform it into a valid signature on another message without knowledge of the signer’s private key. To address this weakness, we propose a minimal countermeasure based on QKD-derived keys and quantum one-time pad encryption.

                                        Abstract
     Designated Verifier Signatures (DVS) are an important variant of digital sig-
     natures that ensure only a specified verifier can validate a signature, while
     preserving non-transferability. With the advent of quantum computing, several
     quantum DVS schemes have been proposed to achieve quantum security. In this
     paper, we revisit the quantum DVS protocol of Xin et al. [Quantum Information
     Processing, 2022 ] and provide a structural cryptanalysis of its design. We show
     that the scheme admits an existential forgery under a chosen-message attack:
     given a valid quantum signature on one message, an adversary can efficiently
     transform it into a valid signature on another message without knowledge of the
     signer’s private key. To address this weakness, we propose a minimal counter-
     measure based on QKD-derived keys and quantum one-time pad encryption. Our
     findings highlight the importance of protocol-level cryptanalysis for the secure
     deployment of quantum information technologies.

     Keywords: Quantum Signatures, Designated Verifier Signatures, Cryptanalysis,
     Quantum One-Way Functions, Quantum One-Time Pad




1 Introduction
The widespread use of the Internet has made secure message authentication and
integrity protection a major concern. The concept of digital signatures, first introduced
by Diffie and Hellman in 1976 [1], addresses this problem by enabling a signer to gen-
erate a signature with a private key that can later be verified using the corresponding


                                             1
public key. Classical digital signature schemes typically rely on hardness assump-
tions such as the discrete logarithm and integer factorization problems. However, the
advent of quantum computing threatens these foundations, since Shor’s algorithm can
efficiently solve both problems.
     To counter this, quantum signature schemes have been proposed, which uti-
lize the principles of quantum mechanics rather than computational hardness. Such
schemes promise security even in the presence of quantum adversaries. Broadly, quan-
tum signature constructions follow two approaches: symmetric-key and public-key.
Symmetric-key variants generally require a trusted third party and often employ tech-
niques such as quantum key distribution or entangled states. Public-key approaches,
first proposed by Gottesman and Chuang [2], are instead based on quantum one-
way functions (QOWFs). Later extensions included the use of single-qubit rotations
and other quantum transformations. Despite their conceptual elegance, several such
proposals have been shown to suffer from structural or security limitations. Notable
improvements were subsequently made through frameworks such as Kawachi et al. [3],
as well as identity-based extensions [4–7] that offer greater flexibility but still depend
on a fully trusted third party. Meanwhile, experimental progress has also been impres-
sive [8–11]. These milestones highlight the growing feasibility of practical quantum
signatures.
     Beyond secure message authentication, quantum signature protocols are expected
to become important building blocks for future quantum information and communi-
cation infrastructures. They can support authenticated communication over quantum
networks, secure distributed quantum computing, quantum cloud services, and other
applications where both quantum information processing and authentication are
required. As experimental quantum communication technologies continue to mature,
ensuring the security of the underlying quantum cryptographic protocols becomes
increasingly important. Consequently, rigorous cryptanalysis of quantum signature
protocols is essential for identifying subtle protocol-level vulnerabilities before their
deployment in practical quantum communication systems.
     A key variant of digital signatures, particularly relevant to applications such as
e-voting and digital contracts, is the Designated Verifier Signature (DVS) scheme.
In DVS, only a specified verifier can validate the authenticity of a message-signature
pair. Crucially, DVS guarantees non-transferability : the designated verifier cannot
convince others of the validity of a signature, as he can always simulate a valid-looking
signature himself. This distinguishes DVS from classical digital signatures, which
inherently provide non-repudiation. The first quantum DVS scheme was proposed by
Shi et al. [12, 13], and several subsequent constructions have followed [14–18, 18–20].
Nonetheless, the design of an efficient and secure quantum DVS scheme remains an
active research problem.

Motivation. While proposing new constructions is important, cryptanalysis of exist-
ing protocols is equally critical for the long-term development of secure primitives.
Careful analysis helps to identify potential weaknesses at an early stage, thereby
preventing insecure schemes from being adopted and informing the design of stronger




                                            2
ones. With the steady growth of quantum DVS proposals in recent years [14–18, 18–
22], it becomes important to rigorously assess their security of quantum DVS. In this
work, we revisit the DVS scheme proposed by Xin et al. [22] and show that it contains
a structural vulnerability that permits signature forgery. We demonstrate how an
adversary can transform a valid signature on one message into a valid signature on
another message, thereby undermining the unforgeability of the scheme. We further
propose a minimal countermeasure that removes the identified vulnerability while
preserving the overall structure of the original protocol. More broadly, this work
highlights the importance of protocol-level cryptanalysis in the development of secure
quantum information technologies, where even subtle design flaws may compromise
the security guarantees of otherwise well-founded quantum primitives.

Our Contribution The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as
follows:
• We revisit the DVS scheme of Xin et al. [22] and point out a structural aspect of
  the design that can be exploited by an adversary.
• We present a concrete forgery attack that allows an adversary who has access to a
  valid message-signature pair to forge a valid signature on another message without
  access to the signer’s private key. We also present a detailed security analysis of Xin
  et al. [22] protocol with respect to other attack models such as replay attacks and
  collusion attacks between dishonest participants. In particular, we have shown that
  Xin et al.’s DVS [22] is also not secure against replay attacks and collusion attacks.
• We further propose a minimal protocol modification based on quantum key distribu-
  tion (QKD), keyed hashing, and quantum one-time pad encryption that eliminates
  the identified forgery attack while preserving the designated-verifier functionality.
  The resulting construction is analysed with respect to the standard security prop-
  erties of designated verifier signatures and compared with existing quantum DVS
  schemes.
Organization of the Paper: Section 1 introduces the problem setting and our moti-
vation for cryptanalysis. Section 2 discusses the preliminaries and standard security
notions for a DVS. Section 3 formally describes Xin et al.’s [22] quantum DVS pro-
tocol; for concreteness, Subsection 3.1 presents a worked toy example that we later
reuse. Section 4 develops our forgery attack in full generality, and Subsection 4.1
demonstrates the attack concretely on the toy instance. Section 4.2 presents a detailed
analysis of Xin et al. [22] with respect to other attack models. Finally, Section 5 dis-
cusses minimal countermeasures based on QKD-derived hashing quantum one-time
pad encryption [23]. In addition, security analysis and performance analysis of the
proposed DVS is described in Section 5.1 and 5.2 respectively.

2 Preliminaries and Security Notions
In this section, we recall the basic syntax and security requirements of a DVS. A DVS
scheme consists of the following algorithms:

                      Setup,   KeyGen,    SignDVS,     VerifyDVS.


                                           3
The signer Anna and the designated verifier Tom generate their respective secret
and public information during the key-generation phase. Given a message m, Anna
runs SignDVS and produces a designated-verifier signature σm . The verifier Tom runs
VerifyDVS on the pair (m, σm ), or on an equivalent protocol-dependent representation
from which the message is recovered, and outputs either accept or reject. A DVS
scheme is correct if, for every honestly generated key pair and every message m, a
signature σm generated honestly by the signer is accepted by the designated verifier.
That is,
                                VerifyDVS(m, σm ) = 1
for every honestly generated signature σm .

We now discuss the security notions of unforgeability and non-transferability. A
detailed discussion on other security notions of DVS can be found in [24–29].

Unforgeability
The unforgeability requirement for a DVS scheme is defined as a security experiment
between an adversary A and a challenger C as follows.
• The challenger C takes a security parameter k and runs cp ← Setup(k ), where cp
  denotes the common public parameters of the scheme.
• The challenger generates the key pairs of the signer and the designated verifier as
  (PKS , SKS ) ← KeyGen(k, cp),      (PKD , SKD ) ← KeyGen(k, cp). It gives cp, PKS ,
  and PKD to the adversary A, while keeping SKS and SKD secret.
• The adversary A may adaptively query a signing oracle on any message mi of its
  choice. For each such query, the challenger returns σi ← Sign(cp, SKS , mi , PKD ).
  The adversary is allowed to make at most qs such signing queries.
• Eventually, A outputs a message–signature pair (m∗ , σ ∗ ). The adversary wins the
  experiment if Verify(cp, PKS , PKD , m∗ , σ ∗ ) = accept, and m∗ was not previously
  submitted to the signing oracle.

Non-transferability
The non-transferability property captures the fact that a DVS signature should not
convince any third party of the signer’s authorship. This is because the designated


                                              4
verifier can generate a simulated signature that is computationally indistinguishable
from a genuine signature produced by the signer. Therefore, any third party will not
be able to determine whether a given DVS signature was produced by the signer or
simulated by the designated verifier.
    Formally, non-transferability is defined through the following game between a
distinguisher D and a challenger C .
• The challenger C takes a security parameter k and runs cp ← Setup(k ), where cp
  denotes the common public parameters.
• The challenger generates the key pairs of the signer and the designated verifier as
  (PKS , SKS ) ← KeyGen(k, cp),         (PKD , SKD ) ← KeyGen(k, cp). It gives cp, PKS ,
  and PKD to the distinguisher D, while keeping SKS and SKD secret.
• The distinguisher D may adaptively make signing queries on messages mi of its
  choice. For each query, the challenger returns σi ← Sign(cp, SKS , mi , PKD ).
• At some point, D submits a fresh challenge message m∗ to C . The challenger chooses

  a random bit b ← − {0, 1}. If b = 0, the challenger computes a genuine DVS signature
  σ ∗ ← Sign(cp, SKS , m∗ , PKD ). If b = 1, the challenger computes a simulated DVS

• After receiving the challenge signature, D may continue to make signing queries,
  but it is not allowed to query the challenge message m∗ .
• Finally, D outputs a bit b′ . The distinguisher wins the game if b′ = b.

4 Forgery Attack on Xin et al. DVS
The security of a quantum cryptographic protocol depends not only on the security of
its underlying quantum primitives but also on the correctness of the protocol composi-
tion. Even when quantum one-way functions and quantum state transmission remain
secure, improper integration of these components may introduce exploitable structural
vulnerabilities. We therefore examine the protocol of Xin et al. [22] from a protocol-
design perspective rather than from the viewpoint of breaking the underlying quantum
assumptions.
    We now revisit the unforgeability argument of Xin et al. [22]. In Section 3.6 of
their paper, Xin et al. argue that an adversary who wants to forge a signature on a
new message m∗ must be able to compute the joint state

                                        |f (a + b)⟩,

which is treated as a secret quantum Diffie–Hellman-type key derived from the quan-
tum public keys |f (a)⟩ and |f (b)⟩. Since this state cannot be computed without
knowing either Anna’s private key a or Tom’s private key b, they conclude that no
quantum adversary can generate a valid forgery.

However, this argument only rules out a from-scratch forgery, where the adversary
attempts to generate a fresh valid signature without having access to any previously
valid message-signature pair. This is not sufficient for the standard unforgeability
requirement of a DVS. As recalled in Section 2, unforgeability must also consider the
case where the adversary is given a valid message-signature pair (m, σm ).
We demonstrate that the quantum DVS scheme of [22] is forgeable. Given a valid
quantum signature on a message m, an adversary can transform it into a valid quantum
signature on another message m̄ without access to Anna’s private key. Hence the
scheme is malleable and does not satisfy the standard unforgeability definition of a
DVS.

4.2 Discussion of Other Attack Models
4.2.1 Collusion-Based Attack
We now discuss a collusion-based attack scenario. This discussion is motivated by
the notion of non-delegatability in DVS. Lipmaa, Wang and Bao [27] introduced

delegatability requires that neither the signer nor the designated verifier should be
able to give a third party a restricted signing capability without revealing the cor-

Having identified the structural weakness responsible for the forgery attack, we now

5.1 Security Analysis
We now discuss the security of the proposed DVS. The purpose of the modification is
not to redesign all components of Xin et al.’s protocol, but to remove the malleability
that enables the message-signature-pair forgery described in Section 4. The remaining
security arguments follow the same structure as in Xin et al.’s scheme [22].

5.1.1 Unforgeability
The proposed modification prevents the forgery attack because the message-dependent
flip pattern is no longer publicly computable. In the original scheme, if an adversary
obtained a valid message-signature pair (m, σm ), then she could compute

                                 h = H (m∥IDA ∥IDT )

and, for any fresh target message m∗ , compute

                                h∗ = H (m∗ ∥IDA ∥IDT ).

She could then modify the quantum signature component by applying Pauli operators
according to h ⊕ h∗ .
In the revised scheme, the flip pattern is computed as

                           h̃ = H (m∥IDA ∥IDT ∥sid∥ρT ∥K ),



                                                15
where K is a secret key shared only between Anna and Tom through QKD, sid is the
session identifier, and ρT is Tom’s fresh nonce. Hence, even if the adversary obtains a
valid signature on m, she cannot compute the correct flip pattern for a fresh message
m∗ , namely
                          h̃∗ = H (m∗ ∥IDA ∥IDT ∥sid∗ ∥ρ∗T ∥K ),
because she does not know K . Therefore, she cannot determine how to transform

                                       |fh̃ (a + b)⟩

into the valid component
                                      |fh̃∗ (a + b)⟩
required for the new message.
Moreover, the message register is encrypted by a quantum one-time pad. The QOTP
keys are derived as
                             (r, s) = KDF(K, h̃∥sid∥ρT ),
and are therefore unknown to the adversary. Thus, even if the adversary tries to alter
the message register, she cannot prepare a valid encrypted encoding of a chosen fresh
message m∗ without knowing the corresponding QOTP keys.
During verification, Tom first recovers the candidate value h̃′ from the quantum
signature component, derives the QOTP keys from

                             (r′ , s′ ) = KDF(K, h̃′ ∥sid∥ρT ),

                           H (m′ ∥IDA ∥IDT ∥sid∥ρT ∥K ) = h̃′ .

Thus, both parts of the signature must be consistent with the same secret keyed value
h̃′ . A previously obtained signature cannot be modified into a valid signature on a new
message unless the adversary can predict the keyed hash/KDF output or break the
underlying quantum one-way construction. Therefore, the proposed countermeasure
prevents the message-signature-pair forgery attack.

5.2 Comparative Analysis
In addition to improving the formal security properties of the protocol, it is also impor-
tant to assess whether the proposed modifications preserve its practical applicability
within quantum communication environments. Since the proposed countermeasure
retains the original protocol structure and introduces only lightweight cryptographic
operations, it can be incorporated into existing implementations with minimal
additional complexity.
    We now provide a comparative analysis of the proposed scheme with existing state-
of-the-art DVS [14, 15, 17, 30–32] in quantum domain. From the viewpoint of key
management, the proposed scheme has a clear advantage over many existing arbitrated
quantum DVS schemes such as [14, 15, 17, 30–32]. In those schemes, the signer and the
designated verifier often have to share their private keys, private quantum states, or
entangled particles with a trusted third party. In our construction, however, the private
keys of Anna and Tom are generated by the users themselves and remain secret with
them throughout the protocol. Hence, no external party is required to store, know,
or distribute the private information of the participants. This feature also eliminates
the key escrow problem. In arbitrated schemes, the security of the users’ private keys
depends on the honesty of the trusted third party, since the TP may possess or help
manage secret information. Such a trust assumption is undesirable in an open network
environment, where no party can be assumed to be fully trustworthy. In contrast, the
proposed quantum public-key DVS scheme does not rely on any TP for protecting the
users’ private keys.
    Unlike many existing quantum DVS schemes, the proposed scheme avoids TP-
related communication overhead and prevents the TP from becoming a bottleneck in
the quantum network. Moreover, the proposed scheme does not require the partic-
ipants to prepare or share entangled particles. This makes the scheme simpler and
more practical than several entanglement-based quantum DVS schemes.

Nevertheless, our cryptanalysis shows that the scheme is not unforgeable. In particular,

new message m∗ without using the private keys of Anna or Tom. Thus, although Xin
et al.[22] satisfies several standard DVS properties, it fails to resist the forgery attack
identified in this work. Moreover, [22] does not prevent the collusion-based attacks
and replay attacks. In contrast, the proposed scheme preserves the positive features
of Xin et al. [22] construction while removing these weaknesses.

6 Conclusion
In this paper, we analyzed the quantum DVS scheme proposed by Xin et al. [22] and
demonstrated that it is vulnerable to an existential forgery under a chosen-message
attack. To address this issue, we proposed a minimal modification in which the signer
and verifier establish a shared secret through QKD, use it to compute a keyed hash, and
protect the message register using a quantum one-time pad. The proposed modification
removes the identified structural vulnerability while preserving the designated-verifier
functionality of the original protocol.
    More broadly, our results emphasize that the security of quantum cryptographic
protocols depends not only on the security of individual quantum primitives but also
on their correct integration within the protocol design. As quantum information tech-
nologies continue to evolve towards practical deployment, rigorous cryptanalysis of
proposed protocols remains indispensable for ensuring their reliability and long-term
security.
